hints: Look at the butamben structure and decide which atom has an available lone pair that can accept a proton without breaking the ester group.
walkthrough:
Spot the basic site**
Think of a base as a proton acceptor. In butamben, $\text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CO}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, the ester oxygens have lone pairs delocalised in carbonyl bonding, but the primary aromatic amine $\text{-NH}_2$ has a lone pair that can pick up $\text{H}^+$. That is where protonation happens.

hints: Compare the availability of the nitrogen lone pair in ammonia with that in an aromatic amine directly attached to a benzene ring.
walkthrough:
Compare lone pair availability**
In ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, the lone pair sits fully on nitrogen, ready to form $\text{NH}_4^+$. In butamben the $\text{-NH}_2$ is attached directly to benzene, so its lone pair overlaps with the ring pi system and is delocalised into the ring. A delocalised pair is much less ready to bond to $\text{H}^+$, so protonation is less favourable and butamben is the weaker base.
Final answer: Weaker base than ammonia because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring and less available to accept $\text{H}^+$.

hints: Recall how strongly the $\text{-NH}_2$ group activates the benzene ring toward $\text{Br}_2(aq)$ and where substitution occurs relative to $\text{-NH}_2$.
Recall what $\text{HNO}_2$ plus $\text{HCl}$ at $5^{\circ}\text{C}$ does to a primary aromatic amine.
Recall what hot $\text{NaOH}(aq)$ under reflux does to an ester group while leaving the aromatic amine intact.
walkthrough:
Bromination is super activated**
The $\text{-NH}_2$ group is very strongly activating, so $\text{Br}_2(aq)$ needs no catalyst and substitutes twice, both positions ortho to $\text{-NH}_2$. That is the 3 and 5 positions relative to the ester group. Keep both the $\text{-NH}_2$ and the $\text{-CO}_2\text{Bu}$ ester unchanged and just add two Br atoms to the ring to give butyl 3,5-dibromo-4-aminobenzoate.

Cold nitrous acid means diazotisation**
$\text{HNO}_2$ with $\text{HCl}$ at $5^{\circ}\text{C}$ converts a primary aromatic amine into a diazonium salt. So $\text{-NH}_2$ becomes $\text{-N}\equiv\text{N}^+$. The ester side chain is untouched. You draw the same butyl ester with $\text{-N}_2^+$ para to $\text{-CO}_2\text{Bu}$.

Hot alkali hydrolyses the ester**
$\text{NaOH}(aq)$ under reflux cleaves the ester linkage by nucleophilic acyl substitution. The acyl part becomes the carboxylate salt $\text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CO}_2^-\text{Na}^+$ and the alkyl part becomes the alcohol butan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. The aromatic $\text{-NH}_2$ does not react under these conditions.

Final answer: With $\text{Br}_2(aq)$: butyl 3,5-dibromo-4-aminobenzoate, $\text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_2\text{Br}_2\text{-CO}_2\text{Bu}$ with Br ortho to $\text{NH}_2$ on both sides.
With $\text{HNO}_2 + \text{HCl}$ at $5^{\circ}\text{C}$: butyl 4-diazobenzoate, $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}^+\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CO}_2\text{Bu}$ para to ester.
With $\text{NaOH}(aq)$ under reflux: sodium 4-aminobenzoate, $\text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CO}_2^-\text{Na}^+$ plus butan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$.

hints: Apply the n+1 rule to the butyl chain $\text{-O-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_3$ and look for $\text{CH}_2$ or $\text{CH}_3$ groups with exactly two protons on adjacent carbons.
walkthrough:
Use n+1 to find triplets**
A triplet means n = 2 neighbouring protons. In $\text{-O-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_3$, the $\text{O-CH}_2$ sees 2 protons on the next $\text{CH}_2$, so n+1 = 3. The terminal $\text{CH}_3$ sees 2 protons on the next $\text{CH}_2$, so n+1 = 3. The two middle $\text{CH}_2$ groups see more neighbours and give larger multiplets. So exactly 2 peaks are triplets.
Final answer: 2 peaks show a triplet splitting pattern.

hints: From (c)(i), identify which two groups in the $\text{-O-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_3$ chain each couple to only one adjacent $\text{CH}_2$ group.
walkthrough:
Pinpoint the two triplet groups**
You found two triplets. One is the $\text{CH}_2$ directly attached to the ester oxygen, $\text{-O-CH}_2\text{-}$, and the other is the terminal methyl, $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_3$. Circle just those protons on the labelled diagram.
Final answer: Circle the $\text{O-CH}_2$ protons ($\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_2$) and the terminal $\text{CH}_3$ protons.

hints: Think about which protons in butamben are attached to N or O and can hydrogen bond, rather than protons attached to carbon.
Recall what happens to labile $\text{N-H}$ protons when shaken with $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ and whether deuterium gives a signal in the proton NMR spectrum.
walkthrough:
Find the exchangeable protons**
Only protons bonded to electronegative atoms like N or O are labile. Butamben has one such group, the aromatic $\text{-NH}_2$. All C-H protons on the ring and butyl chain cannot exchange.

Explain the disappearance**
In $\text{D}_2\text{O}$, the $\text{N-H}$ protons rapidly exchange: $\text{R-NH}_2 + \text{D}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{R-ND}_2 + \text{HOD}$. Deuterium resonates at a completely different frequency, so it gives no peak in the proton spectrum. The $\text{NH}_2$ signal therefore vanishes, leaving one less peak overall.

Final answer: One fewer peak is observed, the $\text{NH}_2$ peak disappears.
$\text{N-H}$ protons are labile and exchange with D from $\text{D}_2\text{O}$: $\text{R-NH}_2 + \text{D}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{R-ND}_2 + \text{HOD}$, and D is not seen in proton NMR.

hints: Calculate fragment masses by splitting at the ester linkage to give an aromatic nitrogen containing piece near m/e 92 and a butyl piece near m/e 57.
walkthrough:
Match masses to cleavages**
Break the molecule at logical points. Loss of the ester side chain leaves $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{NH}_2^+$, mass = $(6 \times 12) + 6 + 14 = 92$. Cleavage of the butyl chain gives the butyl cation $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9^+$, mass = $(4 \times 12) + 9 = 57$. Both are stable positive fragments detected in the mass spectrum.
